passages.t: Masters; prayer; words seasoned with salt
passages.happening:
The household passage ends with masters: “Masters, supply your slaves with what is right and fair, since you know that you also have a Master in heaven” (verse 1).

Then Paul turns to everyone. “Devote yourselves to prayer, being watchful and thankful” (verse 2). Pray for Paul too, “that God may open to us a door for the word, so that we may proclaim the mystery of Christ, for which I am in chains” (verse 3).

And how to live among those outside the church: “Act wisely toward outsiders, redeeming the time. Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how to answer everyone” (verses 5-6).
passages.hearers:
The words to masters would have landed hard in a room where their slaves were listening. ‘What is right and fair’ means treating slaves justly, and the reason is plain: the master is a servant too. He has a Master in heaven, who shows no favouritism (3:25). The owner is not the last word in his house.

Then prayer. ‘Watchful’ means awake and alert, not dozing off. And ‘thankful’ again, as all through the letter.

Notice what Paul asks for himself. Not that the chains come off, but that a door opens for the gospel, and that he will speak it clearly. A prisoner asks for a wider door, not an exit.

The last two verses are about outsiders, the neighbours who did not share their faith. ‘Redeeming the time’ means making the most of every chance. And their words are to be ‘gracious’, kind and full of grace, and ‘seasoned with salt’. In that world the phrase described speech that was lively, well chosen and pleasant to hear. Salt also keeps food from going bad and gives it flavour. Christian speech should be neither bland nor bitter.
passages.ot:
Israel's law protected the worker: “Do not oppress a hired hand who is poor and needy” (Deuteronomy 24:14). And Job knew that master and servant answer to the same Maker (Job 31:13-15).

The open door recalls God's promise in Isaiah: “What he opens no one can shut, and what he shuts no one can open” (Isaiah 22:22).

Salt was part of Israel's offerings: “you shall season each of your grain offerings with salt” (Leviticus 2:13). And Proverbs praises well-chosen words: “A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in settings of silver” (Proverbs 25:11). The psalmist prays, “Set a guard, O LORD, over my mouth” (Psalm 141:3).
passages.asks: Paul tells masters to remember they have a Master. If you have any power over others, ask whether you are right and fair with them. Ask what doors you could pray would open for the gospel where you live and work. And ask whether your words to people outside the church are gracious, and seasoned with salt.

passages.t: Tychicus and Onesimus, faithful and beloved
passages.happening:
“Tychicus will tell you all the news about me. He is a beloved brother, a faithful minister, and a fellow servant in the Lord” (verse 7). “I have sent him to you for this very purpose, that you may know about us, and that he may encourage your hearts” (verse 8).

“With him I am sending Onesimus, our faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you. They will tell you about everything here” (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
There was no public post for ordinary people in the Roman world. Letters were carried by trusted travellers, who often added news in person and helped explain what the letter meant. Tychicus, from the province of Asia, was one of Paul's trusted messengers (Acts 20:4). He carried this letter, and very likely Ephesians too (Ephesians 6:21-22).

With him came Onesimus. Paul calls him ‘our faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you’. That is a remarkable thing to say. Onesimus was a slave from Colossae, almost certainly the same Onesimus the short letter to Philemon is about, who had left his master and met Paul, and had become a believer. Most have thought he ran away; some think he came to Paul to ask for help in a quarrel with his master. Either way, he was going home.

Imagine the church in Colossae hearing this letter read, with Onesimus standing there, and perhaps Philemon, his master, sitting in the room. Paul does not call him ‘the slave’. He calls him ‘brother’, ‘faithful’, ‘beloved’, ‘one of you’. The household passage in chapter 3 is no longer an idea. It has a face.
passages.ot:
The God of Israel loved those whom others counted least, and told his people, “Do not oppress a hired hand who is poor and needy, whether he is a brother or a foreigner” (Deuteronomy 24:14).

And Ruth, a foreigner, found a home among God's people with words of faithful love: “your people will be my people, and your God will be my God” (Ruth 1:16). Onesimus too comes home as one of God's people.
passages.asks: Paul calls a runaway slave ‘faithful and beloved brother’. Ask whether there is anyone in your church you think of by their past or their place rather than as a brother or sister. Ask who might need you to speak up for them, as Paul did for Onesimus. And ask whom you could encourage, as Tychicus was sent to do.

passages.t: Greetings, a word for Archippus, and Paul's own hand
passages.happening:
Paul passes on greetings. Aristarchus, his fellow prisoner; Mark, “the cousin of Barnabas”; and Jesus called Justus. “These are the only Jews among my fellow workers for the kingdom of God, and they have been a comfort to me” (verses 10-11).

“Epaphras, who is one of you and a servant of Christ Jesus, sends you greetings. He is always wrestling in prayer for you, so that you may stand mature and fully assured in the full will of God” (verse 12). Luke, “the beloved physician”, and Demas send greetings too (verse 14).

Greet the believers in Laodicea, “as well as Nympha and the church that meets at her house” (verse 15). Read this letter there, and read the letter from Laodicea (verse 16). “Tell Archippus: ‘See to it that you complete the ministry you have received in the Lord’” (verse 17).

“This greeting is in my own hand—Paul. Remember my chains. Grace be with you” (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
This list of names is a window into the early church.

Mark is the John Mark who had left Paul and Barnabas partway through their first mission, which led to a sharp quarrel between them (Acts 13:13; 15:37-39). Now Paul tells the church to welcome him. The man Paul once refused has become a fellow worker. Broken trust can be mended.

Aristarchus had been with Paul in the riot at Ephesus and on the voyage to Rome (Acts 19:29; 27:2). Luke is named here as a physician; because Paul lists him apart from his Jewish fellow workers, most think Luke was a Gentile. Demas would later leave Paul (2 Timothy 4:10). Faithfulness is not guaranteed by being on a list.

Epaphras is still at work for his home church, from far away, by prayer. Paul calls it ‘wrestling’.

Nympha hosted a church in her house. Churches met in homes, and women like her and Lydia opened theirs. Some later copies have a man's name here, Nymphas, but the woman's name is well supported and widely accepted.

The ‘letter from Laodicea’ has not survived as such. Some think it was the letter we call Ephesians, sent round several churches; others think it was a separate letter now lost.

And the end. Paul usually spoke his letters to a secretary and added the last lines in his own hand. Here the hand that writes the greeting is a chained hand. ‘Remember my chains.’
passages.ot:
Paul's last words, ‘Grace be with you’, carry the spirit of Israel's priestly blessing: “may the LORD cause His face to shine upon you and be gracious to you” (Numbers 6:25).

And friends who sharpen and strengthen one another in God's work are praised in Proverbs: “As iron sharpens iron, so one man sharpens another” (Proverbs 27:17).
passages.asks: Paul's list includes a man he once refused to work with, now welcomed back. Ask whether there is someone you have written off whom God may have changed. Ask who wrestles in prayer for you, and for whom you wrestle. And ask whether there is a ministry you have received and not yet finished, as Archippus was told.
